nameStory: This beautiful bolete is named after Charles Christopher Frost, a 19th-century mycologist from Vermont who was one of the first serious mushroom collectors in New England. It's also called the apple bolete because of its glossy red cap that can look like a shiny red apple sitting among the fallen leaves.
description: Frost's bolete is a stunning mushroom with a dark red, sticky cap that looks almost varnished when fresh. Instead of gills underneath, it has tiny pores that start red and may turn yellow with age. The stem is thick and sturdy with a distinctive net-like pattern, and the whole mushroom will turn blue when you cut or bruise it. It can grow quite large, making it one of the more impressive boletes you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Cut or scratch any part and watch it turn bright blue within minutes - this dramatic color change is the most reliable way to identify Frost's bolete

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Dark red to burgundy, feels sticky or tacky when moist, like touching tape - the surface has an almost varnished appearance that catches light

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Start bright red when young, may fade to yellow-orange with age; look for tiny amber droplets beading on the surface when fresh and moist

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick and solid with a raised net-like or honeycomb pattern covering the upper portion - run your finger over it to feel the texture

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, mild mushroomy smell with no unpleasant or chemical odors

habitat: Look for Frost's bolete in mixed hardwood forests, especially near oak trees where it forms beneficial partnerships with tree roots. It prefers well-drained soil in mature forests and is often found along woodland trails and clearings. In New England, it's most common in lower elevation forests with rich, organic soil.

seasonality.spring: No mushrooms visible yet, but the underground fungal network is beginning to activate as soil warms.
seasonality.summer: Prime season begins in mid to late summer, especially after warm rains - look for the first flushes in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Peak fruiting continues through early fall, with the most abundant finds typically in September before first frost.
seasonality.winter: No mushrooms present, fungus exists only as underground mycelia in partnership with tree roots.

funFact: When fresh and moist, Frost's bolete literally weeps amber-colored tears from its pores - these mysterious droplets appear overnight like dew, but they're actually concentrated compounds the mushroom is actively secreting for unknown reasons.
confusionNotes: Most dangerous confusion is with red-pored, blue-bruising boletes that can be toxic. The sticky, varnish-like cap surface and the distinctive raised net pattern on the stem help distinguish Frost's bolete. Memory trick: 'Sticky red cap with a fishing net stem' - if you can't clearly see both features, don't risk it.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed from Boletus frostii to Exsudoporus frostii - 'exsudoporus' refers to those characteristic amber droplets that 'sweat' from the pores. You may still find this mushroom listed under its old name in older field guides.
compareHints: Frost's bolete is currently the only species in its genus Exsudoporus found in New England, making it unique among our boletes. It differs from other red-capped boletes like the red-cracked bolete by its distinctly sticky cap surface, the amber droplets on fresh pores, and the prominent raised netting on the stem rather than fine lines or smooth texture.
